analogy.p: Imagine the numerator and denominator are two delivery vans, each loaded with parcels (factors) packed inside boxes. If both vans carry an identical box labelled (x + 3), you can take that box out of both and the ratio of the loads is unchanged. But you may only remove a whole box, so you cannot take a single item out of a box that is held together with +, since that is a different load. The analogy breaks down because real parcels run out, whereas algebraic factors are also valid only when the factor is not zero.
analogy.t: Simplifying fractions is like unpacking identical parcels

bullets: The numerator is the top line and the denominator is the bottom line; the fraction bar means 'divide' and also acts like a bracket around each line.
(x + 2)/(x − 3) means (x + 2) ÷ (x − 3), so the top and bottom are each treated as a single block.
An algebraic fraction is only defined when the denominator is **not zero**, so some values of x are excluded.
The five skills are: **simplify**, **multiply**, **divide**, **add or subtract**, and **solve equations** containing fractions.
Edexcel phrases to expect: 'Simplify fully', 'Write as a single fraction in its simplest form', 'Show that' and 'Solve'.
Whenever you see x² in a fraction, expect to factorise it as a quadratic, a difference of two squares or by taking out a common factor.
Link to other topics: factorising quadratics, solving quadratic equations, changing the subject, and speed-distance-time problems.
core.p: An **algebraic fraction** is a fraction in which the numerator, the denominator or both contain algebraic terms, for example 3/(x + 1) or (x² + 5x + 6)/(x² − 9). They obey exactly the same rules as ordinary number fractions, which is why every method in this topic is just 'fractions with letters'. The extra skill is that you must **factorise** before you can cancel, because only **factors** (things multiplied together) can be cancelled, never terms (things added or subtracted). The whole topic therefore rests on factorising fluently, so if your factorising is weak, fix that first.

bullets: **Common factor:** 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3) and x² − 4x = x(x − 4). Take out the highest common factor of every term.
**Difference of two squares:** a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b), so x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3) and 4x² − 25 = (2x − 5)(2x + 5).
**Quadratic with coefficient 1:** x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q) where p × q = c and p + q = b. For x² + 5x + 6 use 2 and 3, giving (x + 2)(x + 3).

**Quadratic with coefficient above 1:** for 2x² + 5x − 3 multiply 2 × (−3) = −6, find numbers that multiply to −6 and add to 5 (6 and −1), split the middle: 2x² + 6x − x − 3 = 2x(x + 3) − 1(x + 3) = (2x − 1)(x + 3).
**Check by expanding:** multiply your brackets back out; if you do not get the original, you made an error.
A sum of squares such as x² + 9 does **not** factorise, so you cannot cancel it.
Spotting a hidden common factor: 2x² − 18 = 2(x² − 9) = 2(x − 3)(x + 3). Always take the number out first.
Mark scheme link: factorising a quadratic correctly usually earns **M1**, so show the brackets even if later work goes wrong.
core.h: The factorising toolkit you need first
core.p: Before any cancelling you must write the top and bottom as **products of brackets**. Four methods cover almost every Higher question. Always start by looking for a **common factor** because it makes later steps easier. Then check for a **difference of two squares**, then a standard quadratic, and finally a harder quadratic where the x² has a coefficient bigger than 1. Practising these until they are automatic is the single best preparation for this topic.

bullets: Step 1: factorise the top. Step 2: factorise the bottom. Step 3: cancel any bracket that appears on both. Step 4: write what is left.
'Simplify fully' means no common factor is left, so check that nothing else cancels.
A second example: (2x² + 5x − 3)/(2x² − 7x + 3). Top = (2x − 1)(x + 3), bottom = (2x − 1)(x − 3), so the answer is **(x + 3)/(x − 3)**.
Numerical factors cancel too: (6x + 12)/(3x + 9) = 6(x + 2)/(3(x + 3)) = 2(x + 2)/(x + 3).
If everything on the top cancels, a **1** remains on the top: (x + 4)/((x + 4)(x − 1)) = 1/(x − 1). Never write 0.
Quick check: substitute a value such as x = 4 into the original and the simplified form; both must give the same number.
Spot the opposite-sign trap: (3 − x)/(x − 3) = −(x − 3)/(x − 3) = **−1**, because (3 − x) = −(x − 3).
Higher extension: you may need to take a factor of −1 out to match brackets, e.g. (5 − x) = −(x − 5).
core.p: To simplify an algebraic fraction you factorise the numerator and the denominator fully and then **cancel common factors**. Cancelling works because dividing the top and bottom by the same non-zero factor does not change the value of the fraction, exactly like 6/9 = (2×3)/(3×3) = 2/3. Example: (x² + 5x + 6)/(x² − 9) = ((x + 2)(x + 3))/((x − 3)(x + 3)) and cancelling the common factor (x + 3) leaves **(x + 2)/(x − 3)**. You must leave the answer in factorised form or as a simplified expression; do not expand it again unless told to.

bullets: Valid: (3x + 6)/3 = 3(x + 2)/3 = x + 2. The 3 is a factor of the whole numerator once factorised.
Invalid: (x + 2)/x ≠ 2 and (x² + 3)/x² ≠ 3. Terms joined by + or − do not cancel.
Invalid: (a + b)/(a + c) ≠ b/c. Only a whole matching bracket or factor cancels.
A power can be reduced: x³/x = x² and (x² − x)/x = x(x − 1)/x = x − 1.
Cancelling the same factor from top and bottom is dividing both by it, which is why the value stays the same.
After factorising, each bracket is a single block: (x + 3) cancels with (x + 3) but not with (x − 3).
Method marks are given for correct factorising even if you then cancel wrongly, so always show the factorised form.
Link: the same idea explains why you cannot 'cancel' within sums in surds or indices work.
core.p: This is the most penalised error in the topic. You may cancel only things that are **multiplied** across the whole numerator and the whole denominator. In (x + 2)/x you cannot cancel the x because the x on top is only one part of an addition. A good test is a number substitution: with x = 4, (x + 2)/x = 6/4 = 1.5, but wrongly 'cancelling' gives 2, which is different. If a bracket is the whole numerator or part of a product, cancel it; if it is added to something, leave it alone.

bullets: Step 1: factorise every numerator and denominator.
Step 2: write as one fraction, or cancel diagonally between different fractions.
Step 3: multiply what remains; leave in factorised form unless the question says 'expand'.
Whole expressions such as 'x' can be written over 1 so that x = x/1 and the rule still works.
Do not multiply out brackets early: it makes cancelling impossible because the common factor disappears.
Check with a value: at x = 4 the original is 4/7 × 7/16 = 28/112 = 1/4 and (x − 3)/x = 1/4, so correct.
Typical mark allocation: 3 marks, with M1 for factorising, M1 for cancelling or combining, A1 for the correct simplified answer.
core.p: To multiply fractions you multiply the numerators together and the denominators together, but with algebra the smart method is to **factorise everything first and cancel across the product** before multiplying out. Cancelling diagonally is allowed because all you are doing is cancelling common factors in the combined numerator and denominator. Example: x/(x + 3) × (x² − 9)/x² = x(x − 3)(x + 3)/((x + 3)x²). Cancelling x and (x + 3) leaves **(x − 3)/x**. Leaving the answer in factorised form is acceptable and usually expected.

bullets: Reciprocal of a/b is b/a; the reciprocal of (x + 2)/(x² + 6x + 9) is (x² + 6x + 9)/(x + 2).
Factorise x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)², which is a **perfect square**; (x + 3)² = (x + 3)(x + 3).
Do the flip before cancelling; people who cancel first often cancel the wrong brackets.
Dividing by an expression: A ÷ (x + 1) is A × 1/(x + 1).
If the answer can be written as a polynomial, the question may ask you to expand it afterwards.
Common error: flipping both fractions or neither.
core.p: Dividing by a fraction is the same as **multiplying by its reciprocal**: keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, and flip the second fraction (Keep, Change, Flip). After that, treat it as a multiplication, factorising and cancelling as before. Example: (x² − 4)/(x + 3) ÷ (x + 2)/(x² + 6x + 9) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x + 3) × (x + 3)²/(x + 2). The (x + 2) cancels and one (x + 3) cancels, leaving **(x − 2)(x + 3)**. You flip only the fraction after the ÷ sign, never the first one.

bullets: Step 1: find a common denominator. Step 2: multiply each numerator by the bracket that its denominator is missing. Step 3: add or subtract the numerators. Step 4: simplify and check whether the numerator factorises and anything cancels.
When the denominators have no common factor, the common denominator is just their product.
Numbers matter too: 1/(2x) + 1/(3x) = 3/(6x) + 2/(6x) = 5/(6x).
Always put brackets round the whole numerator when multiplying: 3(x − 2) not 3x − 2.
Never add the denominators: 1/a + 1/b ≠ 2/(a + b).
'Write as a single fraction' means one fraction bar in your final answer.
Typical mark allocation: 3 marks for adding or subtracting with linear denominators, 4 marks if the numerator needs simplifying and factorising.
core.h: Adding and subtracting: a common denominator
core.p: You can add or subtract fractions only if they have the **same denominator**. So you find a common denominator, rewrite each fraction over it by multiplying top and bottom by whatever is missing, and then combine the numerators. Example: 3/(x + 1) + 2/(x − 2). The common denominator is (x + 1)(x − 2). Rewriting gives 3(x − 2)/((x + 1)(x − 2)) + 2(x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 2)). Add the numerators: 3x − 6 + 2x + 2 = 5x − 4. So the single fraction is **(5x − 4)/((x + 1)(x − 2))**. The denominator is usually left factorised.

bullets: Factorise every denominator first; it reveals shared brackets.
LCD of x and x² is x²; LCD of (x + 1) and (x + 1)² is (x + 1)².
Example with a repeated factor: 2/(x + 3) + 5/(x + 3)² = 2(x + 3)/(x + 3)² + 5/(x + 3)² = (2x + 11)/(x + 3)².
Check 2(x + 3) + 5 = 2x + 6 + 5 = 2x + 11, correct.
If you use a non-lowest denominator, simplify at the end by factorising and cancelling.
Be alert for numerical denominators: 1/(2x) and 1/(4x) have LCD 4x.
This is the main place where a final answer can still be simplified, so check the numerator for a factor equal to a denominator bracket.
core.h: Lowest common denominator and repeated factors
core.p: Using the **lowest** common denominator keeps the algebra small. Factorise each denominator first and build the common denominator from each distinct factor, using the highest power of any factor that appears. Example: 1/(x² − 1) + 1/(x + 1). Since x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), the lowest common denominator is (x − 1)(x + 1). Then 1/((x − 1)(x + 1)) + (x − 1)/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = x/((x − 1)(x + 1)). Using a bigger denominator still works but needs a final cancel to simplify.

bullets: Write the subtraction with brackets on both numerators before expanding.
Expanding − 3(x − 1) gives −3x + 3, not −3x − 3.
For a numerator that becomes a constant, the fraction simplifies nicely, e.g. 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1) = ((x + 1) − (x − 1))/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = 2/((x − 1)(x + 1)).
A negative sign in the denominator: 1/(x − 3) − 1/(3 − x) = 1/(x − 3) + 1/(x − 3) = 2/(x − 3).
Get in the habit of expanding one bracket at a time to avoid sign slips.
Mark scheme: 'M1 for correct common denominator; M1 for correct numerators; A1 for fully correct simplified fraction'.
core.p: When you subtract a fraction, the minus sign applies to the **whole numerator** of the second fraction, so the second numerator must be put in a bracket. Forgetting this changes the signs of some terms and loses accuracy marks. Example: 5/(x − 1) − 3/(x + 2) = (5(x + 2) − 3(x − 1))/((x − 1)(x + 2)) = (5x + 10 − 3x + 3)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) = **(2x + 13)/((x − 1)(x + 2))**. Notice that −3 × −1 gives +3, which students often get wrong.

bullets: Alternative method: combine the top into a single fraction, combine the bottom into a single fraction, then divide using Keep, Change, Flip.
Choose the multiplier as the LCD of every small fraction; here it is xy.
Multiply every term in the numerator and every term in the denominator.
Check with x = 1 and y = 2: top = 1.5, bottom = 0.5, so the fraction = 3. The result (y + x)/(y − x) = 3/1 = 3, correct.
Compound fractions appear most often in Higher 'Show that' questions.
Do not forget brackets around each full numerator when combining.
Link: rearranging formulae where the subject appears in fractions.
core.p: A compound fraction has fractions inside the numerator or denominator, such as (1/x + 1/y)/(1/x − 1/y). The cleanest way to simplify is to multiply the **top and bottom by the common denominator** of all the small fractions. That clears every small fraction at once. Multiplying the top and bottom of the example by xy gives (y + x)/(y − x). Because you multiplied top and bottom by the same thing, the value does not change.

bullets: Multiply **every** term, including terms without a fraction, by the common denominator.
After multiplying, cancel the denominators carefully before expanding.
Cross-multiplication is allowed only when the equation is a single fraction = a single fraction.
Always check solutions in the original equation, especially if you multiplied by an expression involving x.
Reject any solution that makes a denominator zero; it is an excluded value.
Typical marks: 4 to 5 marks, including 1 for the common denominator, 1 for removing fractions, 1 or 2 for solving, 1 for the answers.
If the question says 'Hence solve', use the simplified form from the first part.
core.h: Solving equations that contain algebraic fractions
core.p: To solve an equation containing algebraic fractions, remove the denominators by **multiplying every term by the common denominator** (or cross-multiplying when there is one fraction on each side). Then solve the resulting linear or quadratic equation. Example: 4/(x − 1) = 3/(x + 2). Cross-multiplying gives 4(x + 2) = 3(x − 1), so 4x + 8 = 3x − 3 and **x = −11**. Check: 4/(−12) = −1/3 and 3/(−9) = −1/3.

bullets: Move everything to one side so the quadratic equals 0 before choosing a method.
Choose by inspection: factorise if possible; otherwise the formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a); or complete the square.
Give answers in the form asked: surd form, or decimals to a stated degree of accuracy.
Rejecting solutions: if a solution makes any original denominator zero, say so and discard it.
Interpretation: in a context question one solution is often negative and must be rejected (for example, a negative speed).
Link to quadratic equations and graphs: the solutions are where the curve crosses the x axis.
core.p: Many Higher questions give an equation such as 3/(x + 1) + 2/(x − 2) = 1. Multiplying through by (x + 1)(x − 2) gives 3(x − 2) + 2(x + 1) = (x + 1)(x − 2), so 5x − 4 = x² − x − 2. Rearranging to equal zero gives **x² − 6x + 2 = 0**. This does not factorise, so use the quadratic formula: x = (6 ± √28)/2 = 3 ± √7, which is about 5.65 or 0.35 (to 2 d.p.). Both values are valid because neither makes a denominator zero.

bullets: Denominator zero means the fraction does not exist; you can never divide by zero.
State restrictions only if the question asks for them, for example 'state the values of x for which the expression is not defined'.
To find excluded values, set each original denominator factor equal to zero.
This idea links to graphs of reciprocal functions, which have asymptotes where the denominator is zero.
An equation answer that equals an excluded value is called an extraneous solution and is rejected.
The factor you cancel must be non-zero, which is the logical justification for cancelling.
core.h: Excluded values and what cancelling really means
core.p: Every algebraic fraction has values of x for which it is **undefined**, namely those that make the denominator zero. When you cancel a factor the simplified form is defined at more values than the original, but the two are equal everywhere the original is defined. For example (x² + 5x + 6)/(x² − 9) is undefined at x = 3 and x = −3, whereas (x + 2)/(x − 3) is only undefined at x = 3. At x = −3 the original has a 'hole'; the simplified expression would give 1/6 there. Mark schemes do not usually require this, but it explains why solutions must be checked.

bullets: Time = distance ÷ speed, so a quantity in the denominator of a fraction usually comes from time.
Set up with a clear definition: 'Let x be the speed in km/h'.
Changing the subject: y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) gives y(x − 3) = 2x + 1, then xy − 3y = 2x + 1, then xy − 2x = 3y + 1, so x(y − 2) = 3y + 1 and x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2).
In 'Show that' questions, you must show every line leading to the given answer; do not jump.
Higher extension: algebraic fractions combine with proof (show an expression is always positive) and with inverse functions.
Check final answers using the original wording of the question, including units.
Equation of the form a/(x + p) + b/(x + q) = c nearly always produces a quadratic.
core.h: Algebraic fractions in context and Higher extension
core.p: Algebraic fractions appear in problems about speed, time and work. For example, a 60 km journey at x km/h takes 60/x hours, and the return at (x + 10) km/h takes 60/(x + 10) hours. If the total is 5 hours, 60/x + 60/(x + 10) = 5. Multiplying by x(x + 10) gives 60(x + 10) + 60x = 5x(x + 10), so 5x² − 70x − 600 = 0, so x² − 14x − 120 = 0, so (x − 20)(x + 6) = 0. The speed is **20 km/h** (reject −6). Always reject solutions that make no sense in context.

exam: 'Simplify fully' (3 marks): M1 factorise the numerator, M1 factorise the denominator (or cancel), A1 final simplified fraction. Always show the factorised form.
'Write as a single fraction' (3 or 4 marks): M1 common denominator, M1 numerators over it correctly, A1 simplified numerator, A1 final simplified form if asked.
For 'Solve' with fractions (4 to 5 marks): M1 multiply through by the common denominator, M1 expand brackets, M1 rearrange to quadratic equal to zero, M1 solve, A1 correct values.
'Show that' questions (4 to 5 marks): every line of working must appear; the final line must match the printed result exactly; you earn marks for method, not for the answer.
If the question says 'Give your answers correct to 3 significant figures', use the quadratic formula and write the surd or the unrounded decimal before rounding.
Use brackets in every numerator so signs are not lost; mark schemes allow 'recovery' only if the intended brackets are clear.
Do not expand the denominator in the final answer unless asked; factorised form is accepted and easier to check.
Check your answer with a value: substitute x = 2 or x = 3 into the original and final expressions.
For context questions write what the variable stands for and reject the sensible-impossible root (negative time, speed or length) with a reason.
Command words: 'simplify' = fewer terms; 'express' = rewrite as; 'hence' = use the previous part; 'solve' = find x values.
Time: a 4-mark algebraic fraction question should take about 4 to 5 minutes; do the factorising on the question paper margin to avoid errors.

mistakes.r: Only factors cancel. (x + 2)/x cannot be simplified.
Factorise and cancel first; expanded brackets hide common factors.
Use a common denominator and add numerators only.
mistakes.w: Adding fractions by adding denominators: 1/a + 1/b = 2/(a + b).

mistakes.r: Keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, flip only the second.
mistakes.w: Flipping the wrong fraction when dividing.

mistakes.r: Multiply every term on both sides by the common denominator.
mistakes.w: Multiplying only some terms by the common denominator when solving.

mistakes.r: Reject any answer that makes an original denominator zero.
mistakes.w: Not checking solutions against excluded values.

mistakes.r: When a numerator cancels fully, a 1 remains.
mistakes.w: Writing 0 after everything cancels on top.

mistakes.r: Use the difference of two squares: (x − 3)(x + 3).
mistakes.w: Not factorising the quadratic fully, e.g. x² − 9 left as it is.

summary: The spec asks you to simplify, multiply, divide, add and subtract algebraic fractions, including those needing quadratic factorisation, and to solve equations containing them. It matters because it appears in 'show that' and context questions worth 4 to 6 marks on every Higher paper.

The simplest expression that every denominator divides into exactly.
The fraction turned upside down; the reciprocal of a/b is b/a.

steps: Factorise the numerator: x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3) because 2 × 3 = 6 and 2 + 3 = 5. (M1)
Factorise the denominator using the difference of two squares: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3). (M1)
Write ((x + 2)(x + 3))/((x − 3)(x + 3)) and cancel the common factor (x + 3).
Check with x = 4: original = 42/7 = 6; answer = 6/1 = 6. Correct.

steps: The numerator does not factorise and shares no factor with the denominator, so it is fully simplified.

worked.q: A car travels 60 km at x km/h and returns the same 60 km at (x + 10) km/h. The total time is 5 hours. (a) Show that x² − 14x − 120 = 0. (b) Find the speed x. [5 marks]
steps: (a) Time out = 60/x hours and time back = 60/(x + 10) hours, so 60/x + 60/(x + 10) = 5. (M1)
A speed cannot be negative, so reject x = −6. Check: 60/20 + 60/30 = 3 + 2 = 5. (A1)
